THE DEFENSE: AI ART IS NOT INHERENTLY KITSCH

Argument 1 — Kitsch is a property of use, intention, and reception, not of tools. Kitsch names a relation between a work, its maker, and its audience: work that trades in prefabricated feeling at no risk. A brush cannot be sentimental, a hammer cannot be kitschy, and neither can a diffusion model. The tool may enable kitsch, but the category only takes hold in choices a person makes with it.

Argument 2 — Every new medium was accused of kitsch and later produced genuine art. Photographers were told they merely transcribed nature mechanically; chromolithography, whose cheap sentiment mid-nineteenth century Munich critics helped make "kitsch" a word, was dismissed as soulless reproduction; recorded music was derided as a hollow copy of live performance. In each case the condemnation proved to be about novelty and market access, not inherent value. The pattern counsels humility about pronouncing a new tool incapable of art.

Argument 3 — Human selection, editing, and framing impose risk and friction on AI output. A model generates hundreds of variations; the maker's choice of one over the rest is a judgment, a commitment that stakes something on a particular image meaning something. Discarding the easy, flattering candidates and reshaping what remains reintroduces exactly the friction — the willingness to make a choice that could be a mistake — that separates craft from kitsch. The output is not AI's; it is what a person decides to stand behind.

Argument 4 — Formulaic sentiment long predates AI in human-made commercial art. Greeting cards, vacation-postcard sunsets, and formula pop songs have traded in the most comfortable expected feelings for over a century. If every AI image is kitsch by virtue of predictable feeling, then a large share of deliberate human-made commercial art is kitsch too — which stretches the label so wide it stops meaning anything worth arguing about.

DISCRIMINATING CONDITION
AI art escapes kitsch precisely when the maker bears real risk and judgment — selecting, framing, and revising toward a particular point of view rather than the most comfortable expected image. It remains kitsch when the output is frictionless flattery, engineered to hand the viewer a familiar feeling at no genuine cost to maker or audience.
